name: Coprime Subsequences
description: Let's call a non-empty sequence of positive integers a 1 , a 2 ... a k coprime if the greatest common divisor of all elements of this sequence is equal to 1 . Given an array a consisting of n positive integers, find the number of its coprime subsequences. Since the answer may be very large, print it modulo 10 9 + 7 . Note that two subsequences are considered different if chosen indices are different. For example, in the array [1, 1] there are 3 different subsequences: [1] , [1] and [1, 1] .
input_specification: The first line contains one integer number n ( 1 ≤ n ≤ 100000 ). The second line contains n integer numbers a 1 , a 2 ... a n ( 1 ≤ a i ≤ 100000 ).
output_specification: Print the number of coprime subsequences of a modulo 10 9 + 7 .
approach_summary: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to N using Fermat's Little Theorem (mod 10^9+7 or 998244353). Answer nCr queries in O(1) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 803F — Coprime Subsequences [310. Large Factorials and Binomial Coefficients]
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Combinatorial selection $\binom{N}{K} = \frac{N!}{K!(N-K)!} \pmod P$ can be evaluated in $O(1)$ by precomputing factorials $fact[i] = fact[i-1] \cdot i \pmod P$ and inverse factorials $invFact[i] = invFact[i+1] \cdot (i+1) \pmod P$ using Fermat's Little Theorem $a^{P-2} \equiv a^{-1} \pmod P$.
